As the temperature of the Earth changes, so does sea level. EPA’s Sea Level indicator explains that temperature and sea level are linked for two main reasons: 1) as the total amount of water stored in glaciers and ice sheets on land decreases, it adds to the volume of water in the ocean, and 2) as water warms, it expands slightly. In many coastal locations, sea level can rise more quickly than the global average because the land itself is sinking due to erosion, sediment compaction, natural subsidence (sinking due to geologic changes), groundwater withdrawal, or engineering projects that prevent rivers from naturally depositing sediments along their banks. Rising sea levels increase the flow of salt water into estuaries and nearby groundwater aquifers, contribute to coastal flooding, and make coastal infrastructure more vulnerable to damage from storms. In some locations, sea level can also rise more slowly than the global average due to post-glacial uplift (particularly along the south coast in Alaska).
